metadata.title: Real-world efficacy of lenvatinib/pembrolizumab combination in anaplastic thyroid carcinoma: case series from two Italian referral centers

sections.text: Objective Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (ATC) is an extremely aggressive cancer, traditionally refractory to conventional treatments. The combined therapy with lenvatinib and pembrolizumab (L + P) is supported by a preclinical rationale based on the distinctive immunological profile of ATC. We propose a real-life study to evaluate relevant clinical outcomes and identify survival predictors in a cohort of ATC patients treated with the combined therapy in two Italian referral centers. Methods Sixteen ATC patients treated with the combination of L + P were retrospectively included. Overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), objective response rate (ORR) and disease control rate (DCR) were assessed according to RECIST 1.1 criteria. Baseline patient characteristics, including immuno-nutritional status (calculated using the CONUT score), were analyzed to identify potential predictors of response. Results A median OS of 10 months (95% CI: 4.2–15.9 months) and a median PFS of 6.0 months (95% CI: 0–12.7 months) were observed after L + P therapy. Complete response was observed in 6.2% and partial response in 31.3% of patients, resulting in an ORR of 37.5%; the DCR was 68.8%. Progressive disease occurred in 25% of patients. Furthermore, a baseline CONUT score ≤ 2 resulted in a significantly longer OS (log-rank, P = 0.001) and PFS ( P = 0.05) compared to CONUT score ≥ 3, while a non-significantly longer OS was observed between patients with a baseline ECOG PS of 0–2 and those with a baseline ECOG PS ≥ 3. Conclusion Our study confirms the efficacy and safety of L + P therapy, identifying the CONUT score as a prognostic factor.

Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (ATC) is an extremely rare (1–2 cases per million per year), aggressive tumor arising from thyroid follicular epithelium ( 1 ). It makes up 1–2% of thyroid cancers and can either develop through a dedifferentiation process of a previous differentiated thyroid cancer or arise de novo ( 2 , 3 ). Consistent with its typical rapid growth, resulting in central neck visceral structure compression or infiltration, patients often complain of dysphonia, dysphagia or dyspnea. Indeed, ATC is a life-threatening disease requiring a prompt diagnostic and therapeutic work-up. Surgery has proven to significantly improve overall survival (OS) in patients with intrathyroidal neoplasm or those with locoregional extension suitable for R0/R1 resection ( 4 ). Nevertheless, in unresectable tumors, external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) and/or chemotherapy has, until recently, been the only available but poorly effective treatment options ( 4 ). According to a Dutch nationwide cohort study, including 812 ATC patients, which analyzed OS during the period 1989–2016, before the advent of targeted therapies and immunotherapies, OS was about 2.2 months with a 12% one-year survival, which rose to 21.6% in those without metastases ( 5 ). Since multitarget and highly selective kinase inhibitors (KIs) proved their efficacy in both advanced medullary and radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancers, their potential effectiveness has also been investigated in ATCs, with conflicting results ( 6 , 7 ). To date, clinically meaningful efficacy has been documented only in BRAF-mutant ATCs treated with the highly selective BRAF and MEK inhibitors, dabrafenib and trametinib ( 8 ). However, patients harboring BRAF p.V600E account for up 40% of cases; consequently, the remaining 60% of ATC patients – including RAS -mutated (∼22%) and BRAF wt and RAS wt (∼38%), currently lack effective systemic therapeutic options ( 9 , 10 , 11 ). The ATC immunological profile, largely consistent with that of ‘hot’ tumors, has recently opened new therapeutic perspectives for a neoplasm traditionally refractory to conventional treatments. Indeed, its microenvironment (TME), known to be enriched of anti-inflammatory/pro-tumorigenic (M2-like) tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), tumor-infiltrating leukocytes, cytokines involved in T-cell recruitment and inhibitory immune checkpoint mediators, reflects a cancer immune-escape from antitumor immune response ( 12 ). This peculiar immune landscape, together with an increased tumor mutational burden, and the occurrence of defects in the DNA mismatch repair (dMMR) complex and microsatellite instability, supports the use of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) in this setting ( 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 ). Capdevila et al. first investigated the therapeutic potential of the PD-1 inhibitor spartalizumab in a phase II cohort of 42 ATC patients, revealing modest clinical outcomes, yet demonstrating a positive correlation between PD-L1 expression and treatment response ( 17 ). Since then, the highly selective anti-PD-1, fully humanized, monoclonal immunoglobulin, pembrolizumab, has been the most studied agent in ATC patients, either alone or combined with other treatments ( 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 ). Notably, clinical evidence for its use as monotherapy remains limited, deriving mainly from a small phase II trial enrolling just six patients and few retrospective case series/reports ( 22 , 23 , 24 ) ( ClinicalTrial.gov - NCT02688608 ). Conversely, clinical evidence supporting the use of pembrolizumab in combination with the non-selective KI lenvatinib is more encouraging, being based on results from the phase II clinical trial ATLEP ( 25 ). Indeed, immunomodulatory properties of lenvatinib, over its anti-angiogenic and antiproliferative activities, are thought to enhance the effectiveness of immunotherapy by reducing its primary or acquired resistance ( 26 ). For instance, the preclinical evidence of lenvatinib-induced increase in activated CD8 + T cells and NK cells cytotoxicity, the reduction of Tregs and TAMs and, finally, the inhibition of PD-1, CTLA-4 and TIM3 expression in TME T cells promotes the restoration of exhausted T cell activity, synergistically with ICIs ( 27 ). In Italy, the combined therapy of lenvatinib and pembrolizumab (L + P) is currently reimbursed, under law 648/1996, for the treatment of locally advanced, metastatic and/or recurrent ATCs. Therefore, given the paucity of available real-world data and the limited sample sizes ( 28 , 29 ), we conducted a retrospective study of real-life experience in two Italian reference centers, intended to provide a larger real-world experience following the ATLEP study. The study is aimed at evaluating the main clinical outcomes of patients and at identifying potential clinical or biochemical predictors of response to therapy. Since both disease-related and KI-induced malnutrition is highly prevalent among cancer patients and is associated with negative outcomes, a screening tool to be applied prior to treatment initiation is mandatory in order to optimize prehabilitation strategies before therapy begins ( 30 ). Therefore, we assessed the prognostic role of baseline immune-nutritional status based on CONUT score, an easily applicable score, based on blood parameters (albumin, lymphocyte count and total cholesterol), whose efficacy has already been validated in advanced differentiated thyroid carcinomas treated with multitarget KIs – particularly lenvatinib – and in solid tumors managed with ICIs ( 31 , 32 , 33 ). However, its utility in ATCs treated with combined regimens has not been previously explored.

The study retrospectively evaluated the clinical charts of 16 ATC patients treated with the combined therapy of L + P enrolled in two Italian referral centers, namely Perugia University Hospital and Rome Umberto I University Hospital, between May 2020 and May 2025. Patients enrolled before August 28, 2024 – the date of reimbursement approval by the Italian Medicines Agency (AIFA) – were treated under a compassionate use program, whereas those enrolled thereafter received treatment according to the Italian law 648/1996. The included patients were histopathologically diagnosed with ATCs, either on biopsy or using surgical specimens and received L + P therapy, regardless of treatment line, in either the adjuvant or neoadjuvant setting. Moreover, inclusion criteria foresaw tumors harboring a BRAF wt genotype to be treated in first line with L + P therapy. Patients harboring a BRAF p.V600E mutation could be enrolled only in second-line treatment, after first-line failure of the treatment with dabrafenib and trametinib, as happened in one case. Patients without baseline biochemical data and computed tomography (CT) scan performed prior to L + P initiation were excluded from the study as well as those without biochemical and imaging follow-up assessments. For each patient, the collected baseline characteristics included age, gender, body mass index (BMI), molecular profile, disease stage according to the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) TNM staging system, clinical presentation and treatment-related adverse events (AEs) according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events, version 4.03, based on periodic clinical evaluations and routine laboratory assessments ( 34 ). Furthermore, basal performance status according to Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) scale and basal immune-nutritional status according to CONUT score were evaluated. The latter was computed from serum albumin, lymphocyte count and total cholesterol, obtained by using basal blood analyses collected before the start of the L + P therapy ( Table 1 ) ( 32 ). Based on the CONUT score, the study population was divided into two groups as follows: - CONUT score ≤ 2 (normal nutritional status – light malnutrition) and - CONUT score ≥ 3 (moderate to severe malnutrition).

Response to treatment was assessed by CT or magnetic resonance (MRI) imaging performed at intervals no longer than 3 months, according to the revised RECIST guidelines (version 1.1) ( 35 ). Treatment efficacy was assessed by two time-to-event endpoints, progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS), and two response-based endpoints, objective response rate (ORR) and disease control rate (DCR). PFS and OS were defined as the time from pembrolizumab start to the first evidence of tumor progression or death and the time between pembrolizumab start and death, respectively. ORR and DCR, evaluated in order to assess L + P efficacy in reducing or, at least, in stabilizing tumor burden, were computed as the sum of complete response (CR) and partial response (PR) obtained after L + P therapy and the sum of CR, PR and stable disease (SD) obtained after L + P therapy, respectively. To better elucidate clinical benefit, the duration of response (DoR), for patients who achieved CR or PR, was also calculated as the time from the first response to progression or death; the time to the first response, as the time from treatment start to the first response, and the time to clinical benefit, as the time from treatment start to the first clinical benefit, were recorded.

A univariate analysis was performed to identify factors that affected OS and PFS; variables evaluated included baseline ECOG performance status, baseline CONUT score, molecular profile, stage and treatment with upfront surgery. Kaplan–Meier survival analysis and the log-rank test were used to evaluate the differences in survival between groups. The studies were approved by regional ethical committees – CET Umbria for University of Perugia and CET Lazio 1 for Sapienza University of Rome, and the data were subsequently merged for unified analysis. Written consent was obtained from each patient after full explanation of the purpose and nature of all therapies and procedures used.

The study included 16 ATC patients treated with the combination therapy of L + P in two Italian referral centers. The cohort of patients included 9 females (56.3%) and 7 males (43.7%), with a median age of 66.5 years (IQR: 62.5–75.5 years) and a median BMI of 24.2 kg/m 2 (IQR: 21.6–25.7 kg/m 2 ). Due to the typical rapid growth of the tumor, 12 of 16 cases (75%) were diagnosed because of neck lump, while 6 (37.5%), 4 (25%) and 1 (6.3%) patient complained of dysphonia, dysphagia and dyspnea, respectively. At the time of diagnosis, none of the ATCs was limited to the thyroid. Notably, 7 out of 16 patients had locally advanced disease (stage IVb), while 9 out of 16 patients had metastatic disease (stage IVc). The most frequent metastasis sites were lung (56.3%), mediastinal lymph nodes (12.5%), subcutaneous (6.3%) and bone (6.3%). Although most patients had baseline comorbidities, such as hypertension (68.8%), diabetes (12.5%), autoimmune diseases (6.3%) and other concomitant neoplasms (18.8%), a good baseline performance status was largely observed. Indeed, ECOG performance status (PS) was 0 in 7 patients (43.8%), 1 in 6 patients (37.5%), 2 in 2 patients (12.5%) and 3 in one patient (6.3%). Accordingly, a prevalent good baseline immune-nutritional status was observed, as well. Baseline CONUT score was calculated in 15 of 16 patients (93.7%). Nine out of 15 (60%) had a baseline CONUT score ≤ 2, and 6 patients (40%) had a baseline CONUT score ≥ 3, albeit 4 of the latter showed a baseline CONUT score of 3, resulting in just moderate malnutrition ( Table 2 ).

Once diagnosed, 6 of 16 patients (37.5%) underwent primary tumor surgery. Gene testing was performed in all patients by using either surgical specimens (in those who underwent thyroidectomy) or core needle biopsy (CNB) tissues (in patients with unresectable tumors). All but one of the ATC patients were BRAF p.V600Ewt. Molecular analysis, performed using the Oncomine Precision Assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) at Perugia University Hospital and an in-house NGS-based assay developed and validated at Rome Umberto I University Hospital ( 36 ), revealed mutations in 10 out of 16 patients (62.5%): TP53 mutation was the most common gene alteration (31.3%), followed by NRAS (18.8%), TERTp (12.5%), DNMT3A (6.3%), CCDC6::RET rearrangement (6.3%), BRAF p.V600E (6.3%), EIF1AX (6.3%) and NTRK1 fusion (6.3%) ( Table 3 ).

Lenvatinib therapy was administered at a median dose of 14.3 mg (IQR: 7.2–22.9 mg), while the median starting dose was 18 mg (IQR: 10–24 mg). Pembrolizumab was administered intravenously at the standard dose of 200 mg every three weeks. All but one patient received L + P as the first-line systemic therapy, either as neoadjuvant treatment in 10 patients (62.5%) with unresectable tumors or as treatment for locoregional/distant recurrence in 6 patients (37.5%) previously treated with total thyroidectomy. Notably, 5/6 (83.3%) of the latter, IVc staged, underwent total thyroidectomy for local disease control, while in one IVb-staged patient, total thyroidectomy was performed with curative intent. EBRT was performed in 5/16 (31.3%) patients before L + P therapy initiation. In a single patient with a BRAF p.V600E mutation, combination therapy was initiated after the failure of targeted treatment with dabrafenib and trametinib. The patient harboring CCDC6::RET rearrangement underwent L + P therapy between September 2021 and March 2022. This L + P strategy was adopted over treatment with a selective RET inhibitor since selpercatinib had not yet been approved for thyroid cancer in Italy and available clinical evidence was limited to a single reported case of a CCDC6::RET -rearranged ATC patient enrolled in the LIBRETTO-001 trial ( 37 ). The patient harboring NTRK1 alteration started treatment before the mutational report availability. Given the clinical response, a treatment change was not deemed appropriate. The combined therapy L + P has shown good tolerability. Indeed, although all but one patient experienced either clinical or biochemical AEs according to the CTCAE of any grade, CTCAE ≥ 3 AEs were quite rare. Among the latter, hypertension 2/16 (12.5%), fatigue 1/16 (6.3%), mucositis 1/16 (6.3%) and pharyngeal pain 1/16 (6.3%) were the most common clinical high-grade AEs, while hypocalcemia 2/16 (12.5%), lymphocyte decrease 2/16 (12.5%), γGT increase 2/16 (12.5%), ALT increase 1/16 (6.3%), AST increase 1/16 (6.3%) and anemia 1/16 (6.3%) were the most common biochemical high-grade AEs. One discontinuation of drug was performed for tracheoesophageal fistula, and four dose interruptions were performed for colitis, hemorrhagic alveolitis, cholecystitis and proteinuria. Conversely, considering all grades of AEs, fatigue (43.8%), hypertension (43.8%) and diarrhea (25%) were the most common clinical AEs, while anemia (10/16, 62.5%), hypocalcemia (8/16, 50%), hypercalcemia (7/16, 43.8%) and hyperglycemia (6/16, 37.5%) were the most common biochemical AEs ( Table 4 ).

At the last follow-up, 7/16 (43.8%) patients were still alive with a median OS of 10 months (95% CI: 4.15–15.85 months). The median follow-up was 9 months (IQR: 4–16 months) in the surviving patients. Progression occurred in 11/16 patients (68.8%) with a median PFS of 6.0 months (95% CI: 0–12.7 months) ( Fig. 1 ). According to RECIST 1.1 criteria, a CR was observed in just one patient (6.25%), while PR was observed in 5 out of 16 patients (31.3%) and SD was observed in 5 out of 16 patients (31.3%), resulting in an ORR of 37.5% (95% CI: 15.2–64.5%) and a DCR of 68.8% (95% CI: 41.3–89%). The median time to the first response was 1 month (IQR: 1–2.25 months), while the median time to clinical benefit was 1 month (IQR: 1–3 months). Notably, two patients who achieved PR after L + P underwent total thyroidectomy and EBRT, respectively. The median DoR was 12 months (IQR: 7.5–18 months). Finally, 4 out of 16 patients (25%) experienced PD after L + P initiation, whereas one patient, treated with L + P therapy for locoregional recurrence after total thyroidectomy, achieved disease stability although the lesion could not be defined as target lesion according to RECIST 1.1 ( Table 5 ) ( Fig. 2 ).

sections.section: Survival Predictors In Atc Patients Treated With L + P
sections.text: In this cohort, neither the presence of distant metastases at diagnosis ( P = 0.88) nor the feasibility of upfront surgery ( P = 0.11) predicted OS. Notably, the median OS was 10 months (95% CI: 7.47–12.53 months) in patients not undergoing surgery, whereas it was not reached in those with resected primary tumors, and the difference was not statistically significant, maybe due to the small sample size. Similarly, no significant differences were found for PFS, although patients who underwent surgery had a slightly longer median PFS (11 months; 95% CI: 0–23.5 months vs 4 months; 95% CI: 0–9.51 months). To evaluate the potential correlation between immune-nutritional status and clinical outcomes, the cohort of patients was divided into those with a CONUT ≤ 2 and those with a CONUT ≥3. Notably, disease progression occurred in 6 out of 9 (66.7%) patients in the CONUT 0–2 group with a median PFS of 11 months (95% CI: 2.2–19.8 months) and in 4 out of 6 (66.7%) patients in the CONUT ≥ 3 group, with a median PFS of 1.0 months (95% CI: 0–4.6 months). This translated into a significantly shorter PFS in patients with a poorer baseline immune-nutritional status (CONUT ≥ 3) (log-rank test: P = 0.05). Furthermore, death occurred in 4 of 9 (44.4%) patients in the CONUT 0–2 group, with a median OS of 17.0 months (95% CI: 10.9–23.1 months), and in 4 out of 6 (66.7%) patients in the CONUT ≥ 3 group, with a median OS of 3.00 months (95% CI: 0–6.6 months), resulting in a significantly longer OS in patients with a better baseline immune-nutritional status (CONUT 0–2) (log-rank test: P = 0.001) ( Fig. 3 ). Furthermore, according to ECOG PS, we observed a trend toward poorer survival in patients with a worse baseline performance status. Indeed, a median OS of 13 months (95% CI: 7.30–18–70) was observed in ECOG 0–2 patients, while a median OS of 1 month was observed in patients with an ECOG ≥ 3 (log-rank test: P = 0.064).

The current retrospective analysis describes the largest real-world cohort of ATC patients treated with the combined therapy of L + P since the publication of the phase II trial ATLEP. In our study population, the L + P therapy demonstrated its efficacy across both time-dependent clinical outcomes (median OS of 10 months and median PFS of 6.0 months) and response-based outcomes (ORR of 37.5% and DCR of 68.8%). The clinical control was reached in a median time of 1 month. In addition, the combination regimen was associated with an acceptable tolerability profile, being severe AEs quite rare. These clinical findings, particularly meaningful in the context of BRAF wt ATC patients unsuitable for selective KIs, corroborate the potential efficacy of L + P suggested by preclinical studies and justify its recent introduction into clinical practice ( 8 ). Indeed, this study expands the limited available real-world evidence and adds to the findings of the ATLEP study ( 25 , 28 , 29 ). The latter evaluated L + P efficacy in a cohort of 8 poorly differentiate thyroid cancer (PDTC) and 27 BRAF p.V600E-negative metastatic and mainly pretreated ATC patients. In the ATC cohort, 51.9% PR (14/27) and 44.4% SD (12/27) were observed, resulting in an ORR of 51.9% and in a DCR of 96.3% (26/27). Furthermore, a median PFS of 9.5 months and a median OS of 10.25 months were observed. Consistently, despite a lower median PFS, a superimposable OS of 10 months was observed in our unselected and heterogeneous study population, confirming clearly better outcomes than those reported in historical series ( 5 , 38 ). Notably, since ATC presents as a rapidly evolving and life-threating disease, OS surely embodies the main time-dependent outcome to consider. Therefore, a median 10 month OS supports the long-term effectiveness of L + P in this setting. Furthermore, since prolonged survival was observed even in the few patients who experienced rapid disease progression after treatment initiation, the combination therapy appeared to improve prognosis regardless of the initial morphological response. Moreover, consistent with previous reports, outcomes in our single BRAF -mutated ATC patient who received L + P after the failure of dabrafenib and trametinib further demonstrate the efficacy of the combination therapy ( 39 ). According to RECIST 1.1, SD and PR were the most common morphological responses observed, demonstrating the efficacy of L + P either in inhibiting tumor growth or in reducing tumor burden. Notably, although 31.3% of patients achieved PR – enabling two unresectable ATC patients to become eligible for EBRT and total thyroidectomy – the ORR was only 37.5%, driven by a single CR. Moreover, two-thirds of patients – including those with local tumor recurrence and those with unresectable tumors – experienced clinical benefit through a tumor size stabilization (DCR of 68.8%). This is particularly relevant in the context of ATC, an exceptionally aggressive malignancy, where achieving disease control is a clinically meaningful response-based endpoint. In fact, tumor stabilization can mitigate life-threatening complications caused by the local mass effect on vital cervical structures, thereby providing clinical benefit to the patient. Although both the ORR and the DCR were inferior to the ones observed in the ATLEP study, possibly driven by different lenvatinib doses (starting dose of 18 vs 20 mg of ATLEP – a median dose of 14 mg vs not known of ATLEP), no differences were found in OS. Furthermore, we observed few and mainly slight adverse events, resulting in a general good tolerability of treatment. The favorable tolerability profile, along with a good baseline performance status and immune-nutritional status (see below), likely contributed both to the improved quality of life in our ATC patients and to the effective control of tumor burden. In addition to the objectives outlined above, our study also aimed to evaluate potential clinical or biochemical predictors of disease outcomes. We observed that the immune-nutritional status, assessed by using the CONUT score, emerged as a useful predictor of treatment response, in terms of both OS and PFS. Although based on biochemical parameters, the CONUT score has proven to reflect nutritional and immunological status. Indeed, since tumor-associated lymphocytes are strictly correlated with response to ICI, a lower total lymphocyte count, resulting in a higher CONUT score, is likely to be a marker of impaired immune defenses. Furthermore, hypoalbuminemia is proven to enhance multiple inflammatory factors, such as interleukin-6 (IL-6) and tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α), leading to the progression of tumor inflammation ( 40 ). Finally, cholesterol is considered a marker of both nutritional and immunological status. Although its usefulness as a predictor in solid tumors treated with ICIs has already been assessed, its effect on inflammatory infiltrate is still controversial ( 41 ). Indeed, while some preclinical studies demonstrate a correlation between cholesterol levels and the overexpression of immune checkpoints leading to T cell exhaustion ( 42 ), others show a positive role of cholesterol in the immune response demonstrating its correlation with enhanced NK cell activity ( 43 ). In our study, most patients showed a CONUT score ≤ 2, hence resulting in a prevalent good immune-nutritional status. Furthermore, 13 out of 16 patients (81.3%) showed a good baseline ECOG PS, around 0 or 1. These findings, markers of a general well-being state of the patients, are likely to partially explain the efficacy and the good tolerability over time of L + P combined therapy in our cohort. This real-life, multicenter study included a heterogeneous patient population, likely more representative of the general ATC population than that from clinical trials. Moreover, we evaluated for the first time the CONUT score as a predictor of response to therapy in this subset. The study has a number of limitations, including its retrospective design, the relatively small sample size – which prevented multivariate analysis and resulted in wide CIs for survival analyses, the lack of pembrolizumab monotherapy control arm and the lack of immunological markers to assess potential correlations with clinical outcomes. PD-L1 expression has previously been investigated as a biomarker of response in ATC patients treated with the anti-PD1 spartalizumab therapy ( 17 ). Similarly, Dierks et al. reported improved outcomes in patients with higher PD-L1 expression ( 28 ). However, aside from these reports, little is known about the predictive role of PD-L1 in ATCs treated with lenvatinib and pembrolizumab, given the limited number of published case series. Further studies are therefore warranted to clarify this aspect.

Given the rarity of ATC, our real-life study represents one of the largest cohorts of ATC patients treated with the combination of L + P. This therapeutic strategy demonstrated not only prolonged OS and good tolerability but also the ability to stabilize disease progression, thereby alleviating symptoms associated with rapid tumor growth in the anterior neck compartment and ensuring an acceptable quality of life. Furthermore, our findings suggest that baseline immune-nutritional status may influence treatment response, with the CONUT score emerging as a simple and practical predictive biomarker in this context.
